  • Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I loved journaling as a child. It helped me survive hormonal changes, the usual teen dramas, plus a hefty dose of existential angst. Then college called, and I moved to a different country, leaving behind my childhood, my Nirvana cassettes (I’m old, OK?) and, sadly, my journaling habit.

Recent findings suggest that I made multiple attempts to return to journaling throughout the years, with varying success. I’ve delved into bullet journals under the pretense of improving my productivity, but I gave up when it became too much effort. I’ve invested in multiple notebooks and planners, only to eventually neglect them.

Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer.

It all began when I discovered the wondrous world of journaling TikTok. In short-form videos, creators would show off beautiful journal pages decorated with colored markers, stickers, washi tape and, yes, photos — specifically photos from portable printers because the prints are small enough to fit within the confines of a typical journal or planner. I really liked the idea of decking out my journal pages with photos of my everyday life. I knew I had to get one.

Industry observers note that after a bit of research, I decided on a couple of criteria. First, I wanted the printer to be a dye sublimation printer rather than a ZINK (Zero Ink) printer. Dye sublimation printers essentially use heat to transfer dye onto the paper, while ZINK printers use a special paper that activates under heat with no ink required (hence the name). Dye sublimation prints tend to be higher quality because it transfers the dye in layers of cyan, magenta and yellow, followed by a protective coating.

Second, I wanted the photo to be on sticky paper so that I didn’t have to mess around with glue to add these photos to my journal.

I found quite a number of dye sublimation pocket printers on the market, but the one that caught my eye immediately was the Polaroid Hi-Print 2×3 Generation 2 pocket printer. I fell in love with it the moment I saw it. The sleek white design, the Polaroid logo and that curved rainbow accent on the edge really sealed the deal for me. Call me a sucker for style, I guess.

According to recent reports, I purchased a Hi-Print 2×3 “starter set,” which includes the printer along with two 2×3 paper cartridges. Each cartridge has 10 photo sheets, and each sheet is made out of sticky back photo paper, which is exactly what I wanted. Both the Gen 2 and the prior Gen 1 are easy to find; the main difference is the newer one uses a USB-C charging port while the original uses the older Micro-USB port.

Getting started with the printer is simple enough: Download the Polaroid Hi-Print app, pair the printer with your phone and you’re ready to go. The app is fairly easy to navigate. I like that it lets you arrange your photos in collages so you’re not limited to just one photo per sheet. You can also decorate your prints with colorful frames or decorations. The printer even offers a mosaic option that lets you print out one major image using multiple sheets.

In a recent development, since it’s a dye sublimation printer, the Hi-Print prints out photos in stages. It lays down the different colors in multiple passes (yellow in the first pass, magenta in the second pass, and so forth). Because of that, printing does take a while: around 60 seconds per photo.

Industry observers note that but I don’t mind the delay, as the resulting photo quality is superb. The colors are vibrant and the overall image is nice and sharp. The contrast could be a little better, but for a little pocket printer, the quality definitely exceeded my expectations.

There are a few downsides, however. The obvious one is that photo cartridges can be pretty expensive. One pack of 20 sheets is around $17, though you can get it for $14 each if you buy the 5-pack. That’s still almost 70 cents per 2×3 print. If you use multiple prints, that can add up pretty quickly.

Another downside is that it doesn’t have a super long battery life. It only has a 620mAh battery, which Polaroid notes will last up to 20 photo printing sessions. I only ever use this printer at home, so this isn’t a major deal for me, but I can see this being a potential disappointment if you want to bring this printer on the road. That remarked, if you do want to charge it, it doesn’t take that long. Polaroid says it takes under an hour, and that feels about right based on my experience.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had this printer for a few months now, and I’m very pleased with it. Since I use the photos primarily with my journal, I also really appreciate how thin the photo sheets are, so they don’t bulk up the pages too much. I truly enjoy printing out my little creations, cutting out my collages and then decorating my journal with them.

I might not have my childhood back nor my Nirvana cassettes, but at least I’ve finally recaptured the joys of journaling — even if it did require a bit of help from a pocket printer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you picked up a latest iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

It has been revealed that the ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Recent findings suggest that both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR indicates it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

Industry observers note that on these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Why it matters: ESR indicates the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing demonstrates up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Installation is the part most people dread on a brand-new iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and noted it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

It has been revealed that it’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR notes it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

In a recent development, for the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

According to recent reports, ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

The trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the new M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

Have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

According to recent reports, when the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR states the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

The result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

The ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

The ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

The best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

Sources indicate that ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the fresh iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft indicates its newly introduced AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

In a recent development, earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

According to recent reports, software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Sources indicate that then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s fresh.

It has been revealed that what comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

Industry observers note that in other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

In a recent development, microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the organization’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

This means the tech giant doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

#96800. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2231 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.
  • But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto.
  • Something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some complications. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these problems, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Industry observers note that adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

Sources indicate that if it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a major or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

According to recent reports, when I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”.

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand remarked.

It has been revealed that things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning last week.

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers indicates CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers remarked.

Sources indicate that despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” mentioned Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

Recent findings suggest that AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

Sources indicate that the good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Substantial Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”.

Sources indicate that and defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”.

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

In a recent development, that’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security problems in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” mentioned Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity manufacturer focused on connected devices.

According to recent reports, it goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of problems is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to patch so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

Industry observers note that and patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s challenges on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing problem.

Industry observers note that in the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

According to recent reports, substantial Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” noted Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy indicates.

According to recent reports, that means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into latest software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

Recent findings suggest that the main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

According to recent reports, “I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”.

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more notable than ever.

Recent findings suggest that “You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers remarked. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”.

In a recent development, but consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a company isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection.

It has been revealed that we don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella confirmed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft claims its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella confirmed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft claims its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several upcoming Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft remarked, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

It has been revealed that the firm added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also revealed a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up promptly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

In a recent development, microsoft also declared that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft unveiled last year, is the organization’s observability platform. Microsoft remarked Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a fresh way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft stated. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise looks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing.

A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.

In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

Though doctors have remarked the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.

Industry observers note that half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.

Sources indicate that patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.

A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.

Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in Fresh York, who presented the findings, stated “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.

He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.

“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.

There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.

Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.

“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”.

One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago.
  • Recent findings suggest that how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo?
  • Industry observers note that I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago. Every day since then, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, a dedicated machine inside CNET’s lab has been folding and unfolding it over and over again. For science.

Recent findings suggest that how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of Friday, Nov. 20, we’re up to more than 565,000 folds and the Duo hasn’t broken yet. The hinge has shown signs of potential failure, however. Our technicians, as well as the cameras and sensors that are part of our testing rig, continue to monitor the situation and collect data.

Industry observers note that I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built this proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close, over and over, for the past few weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review as well as her one-month-later follow-up. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Sources indicate that join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

According to recent reports, most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.).

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

It has been revealed that in conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

In a recent development, we also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

Sources indicate that to secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

Industry observers note that there’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

According to recent reports, apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella unveiled several newly introduced models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the tech giant. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft indicates its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.

Recent findings suggest that MAI remarked it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Manufacturer to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, mentioned during the keynote.

Industry observers note that the approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft remarked it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman noted during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the firm has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the newly introduced coding model the manufacturer unveiled at Ignite.

According to recent reports, the organization also released its fresh image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

Three women in their late 30s reunite for the funeral of a childhood friend, only to start suspecting her death was no accident. That’s how “How to Get to Heaven from Belfast” opens — and it might just be the funniest, most underrated show most people never bothered to watch this year.

It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year. The show comes from Lisa McGee, the creator of the beloved “Derry Girls,” though you shouldn't walk in expecting more Catholic-schoolgirl hijinks. This is a darker, twistier beast: a genuine murder mystery that happens to be laugh-out-loud funny, trading teenage chaos for middle-aged mayhem. Across eight tightly wound episodes, McGee’s razor-sharp writing and a trio of electric lead performances turn a simple whodunit into a story about grief, friendship, and the secrets we bury—all set to a killer ’90s soundtrack.

If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.

In a recent development, saoirse (Roisin Gallagher), Robyn (Sinéad Keenan), and Dara (Caoilfhionn Dunne) were inseparable as teenagers in Belfast, part of a tight-knit group of four. Now in their late 30s, they’ve drifted apart and moved on with their lives — until the sudden death of the fourth member of their group, Greta, brings them back together for her funeral.

In a recent development, what should be a simple reunion rapidly spirals into something a lot weirder. The women start to suspect that Greta’s death wasn’t the accident everyone’s calling it. In fact, it may tie directly to a secret from their shared past, one they’ve spent years trying to forget.

Determined to find out what really happened, the trio releases an investigation that takes them well beyond Belfast — even landing them at a resort in Portugal — as the past they’ve been outrunning finally catches up with them.

Industry observers note that I’ll keep this simple: The show is funny, the mystery is sharp and the two actually work in tandem. Most of the credit goes to Lisa McGee’s writing. She pulled off the same balancing act on “Derry Girls,” where the comedy never undercut the emotional gut-punches. Doing it again here with older characters and darker stakes makes the show feel far more grounded than most mysteries in its lane.

According to recent reports, roisin Gallagher, Sinéad Keenan, and Caoilfhionn Dunne play women who’ve known each other since childhood, and you buy it immediately. They bicker, cover for each other, and slip back into old habits the way real lifelong friends do. Their chemistry is electric—and given how much time they spent together on set, it’s easy to believe that bond carried over off-camera.

Best of all, it’s a self-contained eight-episode miniseries, meaning the whole story is here and it actually has an ending—no cliffhangers. You can knock it out in a weekend without worrying about Netflix abruptly pulling the plug on a resolution.

According to recent reports, it didn’t get nearly the attention it deserved the first time around, which is exactly why it’s worth seeking out now. If you want a smart, funny mystery you can start and finish without a massive commitment, it’s streaming on Netflix — so make sure to catch it (and “Derry Girls” too, if you haven't already).

  • The Gemini AI improvements got a real-world test during Washington state’s Railroad Fire in July 2026, when Watch Duty issued what it calls its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert.
  • “This is something the tool also has the capability to do if reports of flooding are communicated via radio,” said Dave Merritt, co-founder and chief technology officer of Watch Duty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Friday, Google’s Gemini team declared the results of a new partnership with the wildfire-tracking app Watch Duty, after Gemini engineers spent six months embedded with Watch Duty’s first responders. The results cut vital new wildfire dispatch translations down to seconds and helped improve radio communications, which can be rough on the front lines of a new fire.

The Gemini AI improvements got a real-world test during Washington state’s Railroad Fire in July 2026, when Watch Duty issued what it calls its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert. The alert stemmed from a nearly unintelligible, static-filled 911 call that the Gemini tool transcribed in under 30 seconds. That kind of assistance can help Watch Duty send alerts to affected communities more quickly and enable first responders to revision maps more accurately and make better-informed decisions.

“This is something the tool also has the capability to do if reports of flooding are communicated via radio,” said Dave Merritt, co-founder and chief technology officer of Watch Duty. “Across disasters, we hear feedback every day that first responders are using Watch Duty for additional situational awareness, especially for disasters that span multiple counties.”.

Watch Duty reporters are active and retired first responders who can manually monitor up to 20 different feeds, though static and rapid-fire jargon can make them difficult to follow.

Gemini workers used more than 20,000 hours of Watch Duty radio recordings to train the AI tool to recognize firefighting terms that aren’t in the average dictionary or books that AIs are typically trained on.

Google says the tool is not designed to replace human decision-making in life-or-death situations.

“This tool takes on the demanding work of listening, freeing Watch Duty’s volunteers to focus on what matters most: confirming fires and getting warnings to people while they can still act,” remarked Stephanie Chew, Google project team lead.

The project was completed at no cost thanks to a Google.org fellowship, and the resulting Watch Duty app features are free to use.

From the data collected, Gemini engineers and Watch Duty identified several measures of success.

Industry observers note that one metric was the word error rate, which fell by around 15% after the AI model was implemented. Another sign of success was a jump in Watch Duty volunteers’ satisfaction with their radio transcription tools, from around 35% to 92%.

Sources indicate that the Gemini tool continues to analyze approximately 200 hours of radio speech traffic from 400 feeds per day. The tool was made to handle more than 10,000 radio feeds if necessary.

The integration could pave the way for broader use across public safety. The platform’s built-in scalability could eventually bring similar audio-clearing tools to local fire departments, 911 call centers and Coast Guard operations, where clear communication is critical under pressure.

In a recent development, ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

Sources indicate that but what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet.

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

Industry observers note that this is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

It has been revealed that also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why.

And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big issue for many people.
  • You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself.
  • With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are key for sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big issue for many people. Which is why, if you've found yourself repeatedly awake at 3 a.m. and unable to fall back to sleep, it's time to take a look around your bedroom.

You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself. The simple act of removing them might be the difference between another broken night's rest and staying asleep all night.

With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are key for sleep.

Temperature, light and sound pollution can all stop you from staying asleep all night."People sleep better when it's dark, when it's quiet, when it's cool, when it's free of disturbances [and] when it's safe, indicates Dr. Aric Prather, sleep scientist and expert at UCSF and BetterSleep. "And so, trying to optimize that environment on those facets, is certainly a step towards a better night of sleep.".

Sources indicate that while 3 a.m. wake ups have a variety of causes, there are environmental factors that can contribute to them happening, and keep you awake. Here, we explain what they are, and how removing certain items from your room can help.

In a recent development, both experts we spoke to advised, where possible, to keep work outside of the bedroom. And since many of us work on computers or laptops at home, removing these from your sleep space can help eliminate distracting light sources and potential stress they're associated with.

The Sleep Foundation points out that having electronics near the bed can contribute to nighttime wakeups through the noise and light they can emit. So, we asked Heather Darwall-Smith, a UKCP psychotherapist specializing in sleep and author of The Science of Sleep, if laptops in the bedroom can be impactful on sleep, through the association with work or light from charging cables.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Recent findings suggest that if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'.

"It's both," she notes. "The mind needs to know the day is done. It's like putting work away. It's creating that boundary between work and home," she explains.

Dr. Prather also points out that waking and seeing a light from a laptop charging cable can carry anxiety. "Because if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'" he indicates, adding that it can also lead to ruminating over the next day being a work day.

He adds that "some people's computers have fans that are constantly running and there's heat coming out of them. So that can change the the temperature of the room or the temperature near their body.".

As temperatures drop over the winter, keeping your heating on overnight can appear to be a sensible way to combat the seasonal chill — but being mindful of temperature is key to avoiding waking up.

“High temperatures in your bedroom can interfere with your body’s natural cooling process, which is essential for falling and staying asleep,” Dr. Hannah Patel previously explained.

But turning your heating off in the lead-up to bedtime — ideally anytime from around 9 p.m. (though that's not a hard and fast rule if you're an early bird or a night owl!) — you'll allow your bedroom time to cool down.

Similarly, sleeping with an electric blanket is another nighttime practice to be particularly careful with.

Not only is it unsafe to keep an electric blanket on all night (the Electrical Safety Foundation International claims they should never be used while sleeping), even modern models with built-in protection to prevent overheating, advise turning off before falling asleep.

Removing your phone from the bedroom is something the Tom's Guide sleep team swears by, in part because expert advice suggests that scrolling your phone late at night can cause a state of mental arousal that may lead to disrupted sleep.

Not to mention, a recent study found that every hour spent on screens before bedtime increases the risk of insomnia by a whopping 59%. As Dr. Prather points out, "phones on their own aren't really problematic, but if people can't keep their hands off them, then they are.".

And while the jury is still out on how much blue light from screens is really going to affect your sleep, looking through your phone in the middle of the night can stimulate your brain and prolong awakenings.

However, Darwall-Smith notes that she often finds "people are more stressed by taking the phone out of the bedroom than having it there.".

If that's you, consider "turning off your notifications, thinking about how checking the screen or getting into live activity on your phone is going to keep you awake," the sleep psychotherapist advises.

It's the literal foundation of your sleep, but you might not have considered that your mattress could be playing a significant part in disrupting it.

Waking up with back pain or stiffness, aching shoulders and hips, overheating during the night, tossing and turning, and even waking up coughing and sneezing can all be signs that your mattress is the culprit behind your nighttime wake ups.

"If you're constantly having back pain or your mattress isn't okay... look into it," claims Darwall-Smith, though she points out that back pain might be caused by factors outside of your mattress.

Dr. Prather suggests finding a mattress that is "the right comfort for you, and that probably changes as you age," and recommends "one that supports your posture [and] that doesn't cause pain.".

However, as Darwall-Smith notes, "sometimes it's not in [people's] control to change their mattress. So what can you do to make the mattress comfortable? You might want a topper." The best mattress toppers can adjust the comfort and feel of your mattress, and even help with regulating the temperature, all without the cost involved in replacing your existing bed.

Having the wrong pillow for your sleep position, one that has lost it's shape and support, is aggravating allergies or is causing neck pain can all contribute to nighttime wakeups.

Sources indicate that research shows a relationship between an uncomfortable pillow and poor sleep. One study looking at pillow performance found that everyone "who reported poor sleep quality also reported poor pillow comfort.".

Sheets, meanwhile, might be something of an afterthought, but synthetic fabrics can trap heat and cause sweaty wake-ups — even though the often low price-point can seem attractive.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Prather indicates that along with the right mattress, "the quality of the sheets," and their "breathability" as well as "the quality of the pillow, can all contribute to how comfortable people are, and certainly comfort is something that we want to foster when we're trying to get people to sleep well.".

Our best pillows of 2026 can help you determine what's right for you and our guide to the best bed sheets sets of the year has options for different sleep preferences, seasons, and budgets.

While a basic alarm clock can be a better option that relying on your phone, if it's visible from your bed it's potentially making nighttime wakeups worse.

It has been revealed that "I prefer people to use actual alarm clocks and to try and find non-alarming alarm clocks," says Darwall-Smith. However, she adds that "I prefer people not to look at their clock.".

According to research, clock-watching or 'time monitoring behaviour' (TMB) is common in people who experience insomnia, and something that perpetuates the symptoms of the condition.

Sources indicate that looking at the clock when you wake during the night is "only bad news" says Dr. Prather. "I deal with people with insomnia, but most people are looking at the clock hoping that it's later in the night than it is. And they're almost always wrong.".

Being aware that it's not as late as you hoped then leads to "an immediate anxiety or frustration or discouragement, which pushes against falling back asleep," he explains.

Obviously, we're not suggesting getting rid of the main light in your bedroom altogether, and living each evening in a state of complete darkness.

But if you find yourself awake during the night? "You should not turn on big lights," claims Dr. Prather. "If you can keep it low light, that's certainly better.".

Speaking of light at night, Darwall-Smith explains that "if you're shining light into your brain at 4 a.m., that's not [good]. Because sleep is reset by the light-dark cycle. As we push towards wakefulness, our eyes register light and it's part of what pushes us up into [being] awake.".

However, Dr. Prather cautions against "[sitting] in the dark with your thoughts, usually that isn't a good solution." He recommends activities that are sleep supportive, relaxing and distracting, like reading with a book light, or using a Kindle on low intensity.

Being wide awake in the middle of the night is rarely pleasant, but you don't always have to be concerned by a brief awakening.

"Waking up during the night is normal... it's part of sleep structure. Especially as people get older, it would be very uncommon for people to not wake up during the middle of the night," says Dr. Prather.

Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend.

According to recent reports, darwall-Smith agrees, adding that, "What we're looking at is the quality of what that waking is. If you get up, wander around, go and have a pee, go back to bed, happy days. You get up and your eyes are peeled to the ceiling and you're freaking out, not so happy days.".

And though we've covered ways you can help your sleep by adjusting your bedroom environment, the experts we spoke to emphasized focusing on what works for you, and not adding stress by focusing on creating a 'perfect' environment. "We're not looking for perfection. We're looking for good enough to sleep better," says Dr. Prather.

Darwall-Smith agrees: "Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend. And if we're rushing around trying to perfect our sleeping conditions, Well, do we really need to? Good enough is good enough.".

According to recent reports, we've talked about what to remove, but there are useful products which can help tackle issues with noise, light and comfort that may be impacting your night's rest. You don't need to strive for absolute perfection, consider these as tools for a calmer, more relaxing night. Even better, these three items are all reduced in the Black Friday mattress deals.

iOS 27.3 Could Bring the Redesigned Health App and a More Capable Siri AI to Your Device Soon
